en: The Sūtra on the Inner Treasury of a Hundred Jewels, translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Later Han Dynasty.
At that time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. There were twelve thousand bhikṣus present.
The assembly of seventy-two thousand monks and bodhisattvas sat together.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
"In this great assembly of bodhisattvas, we wish to hear from the Buddha concerning the matters entered into through *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means)."
"For what cause and condition does a bodhisattva analytically know internal and external phenomena?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī: "Listen to what I say.

One enters the teaching by following worldly customs; the Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and the sūtras and dharmas are beyond calculation. They cannot be known by any arhats or pratyekabuddhas, let alone by those people of the world who might hear or know them."

The conduct of worldly people is characterized by attachment, whereas the conduct of the Buddha is free from all attachment; only a Buddha can truly know another Buddha, as described in the Buddha’s sūtras and dharmas, and as reflected in the inner and outer mental wisdom of a Buddha’s own body.
"For what reason does the Buddha appear in the world?
By what cause should he be specifically known?
Though dwelling in the world, he is unattached to all things; he acts as a light for the entire world."

In his bodily conduct, verbal expression, and mental reflections, he conforms to worldly customs and enters among them; yet he practices internal affairs and all the Buddha-dharmas. His practice is such that none can surpass it, and his Buddha-practice is such that none can reach it. While conforming to worldly customs, there is no one who can fully comprehend him.
“Because the Buddha has compassion for the people of the ten directions, he manifests light everywhere; according to what the world delights in, he preaches the Dharma.

A bodhisattva is not born from the union of the parents' vital essences; his body is a transformation, like a magical illusion that manifests parents. He enters into accordance with worldly customs and manifests himself in this way.”
“The Buddha’s radiant flames are incalculable, illuminating the ten directions; yet he enters according to worldly customs and manifests a radiance of seven feet.
The Buddha never actually places his feet upon the ground, yet the marks appear as if they were touching it; he manifests such things by entering according to worldly customs.”
"Since tens of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas past, the Buddha has accomplished the *prajñāpāramitā*; yet, conforming to worldly customs, he manifests as a child."
"The Buddha illuminates the people of the ten directions who dwell in the darkness of lust; he enters according to the worldly customs and likewise manifests as having a wife and children.
When the Bodhisattva was born and fell to the ground, he spoke of himself, saying:
'In the heavens above and the earth below, there is none who surpasses me; I shall deliver the people of the ten directions.'"
Conforming to worldly customs, he likewise questioned the Prince regarding his time sitting beneath the tree in Jambudvīpa;
how he rose from there and practiced austerities for six years, conforming to worldly customs to manifest such diligent suffering to people.
"When the Buddha’s Way was about to be perfected, he sat alone beneath a tree; conforming to worldly customs, he emitted light so that Māra would know of it.
Once the Buddha’s wisdom was fully realized—equal in all respects and unsurpassed—he conformed to worldly customs and attained the peaceful seat of Buddhahood, manifesting such things to the world."
"Although he has attained Buddhahood, out of compassion for the people of the ten directions, he shall preach the sutras to deliver them.
Śakra and Brahmā entreated the Buddha with compassion, requesting him to preach the sutras for the sake of humanity; thus, conforming to worldly customs, he manifested himself in this way."
“The Buddha’s wisdom can neither increase nor decrease; it is only in accordance with worldly conventions that he manifests such variations in the extent of his wisdom.

The Buddha likewise comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, abiding as he originally was; yet, in accordance with worldly conventions, people speak of the Buddha ‘coming and going,’ and he manifests himself in this way.”

“The Buddha has no place of entry or abode; he is like space, which likewise has no place of entry or abode. Yet, conforming to worldly conventions, people call the Buddha ‘abiding,’ and he manifests himself in such a way.”
"The Buddha's feet are like lotus flowers; they do not receive dust or grime. When the Buddha washes his feet, he does so by conforming to worldly customs, manifesting it in this way."
“The Buddha’s body is like gold and does not receive dust or grime; yet the Buddha manifests entering the bath, doing so in accordance with worldly customs—thus he demonstrates this.

The Buddha’s mouth is fundamentally pure and clean, like the fragrance of saffron; yet the Buddha uses a willow branch to rinse his mouth, doing so in accordance with worldly customs—thus he demonstrates this.”
"The Buddha has never experienced hunger; however, out of compassion for the people of the ten directions, he manifests hunger as a way of conforming to worldly customs, appearing in such a manner."

“The Buddha’s body is like a vajra—pure, stainless, and free from excrement or urine; yet he manifests the passing of small and large excrement to people, entering according to worldly customs and manifesting in such a manner.”

“The Buddha’s body never undergoes aging or decay; it possesses only manifold virtues. Yet he manifests an aged body, conforming to the worldly customs and conventions, and thus displays such a manifestation.”

"The Buddha's body has never been subject to illness, yet he manifests sickness, calls for physicians, and takes medicine; those who provide him with medicine obtain immeasurable merit. He acts in this manner by conforming to worldly customs and entering into them."

"The power of the Buddha is irresistible; he can move the buddha-fields of the ten directions with a single finger, yet he manifests to people as emaciated and utterly exhausted, entering into the worldly customs and manifesting himself in such a way."

“In a single moment of thought, the Buddha can fly to countless buddha-fields, yet he manifests extreme exhaustion; this is how he enters into accordance with worldly customs and makes such a display.”

“The Buddha’s body is like an illusion; it takes the name of the Dharma as its body, yet manifests as a body of impurities to people. It enters according to worldly customs and manifests in such a manner.”
"The Buddha is fundamentally non-existent; he manifests existence according to what the world delights in, entering into worldly customs and manifesting in such a way."

"The power of the Buddha’s body is immeasurable; ultimately, there is no sitting, rising, walking, or lying down, yet he manifests sitting, rising, walking, and lying down to people. He enters according to the worldly customs and manifests in such a manner."
“The Buddha’s body is never moved by cold or heat; yet, in accordance with whatever cold or heat or cool shade he encounters, he enters into the worldly customs and manifests himself in such a way.”

“The Buddha is like space; he appears to people as one who is always clothed and never disrobes. It is, for example, like the devas of the Brahma realm who are always clothed; he manifests in this way by conforming to worldly customs.”

“The Buddha’s head has never lost a hair; the Dharma merely demonstrates this to people, and there is no one who sees him taking a razor and departing. He enters according to worldly customs and manifests in such a manner.”
“The Buddha has no time when he is not seated; yet he manifests sitting upon stone, undergoing diligent hardship, entering in accordance with worldly customs, and manifesting in this way.

The Buddha possesses the mark of the flavor of ambrosia in his throat and has never known hunger; however, out of compassion for the people of the ten directions, he accepts whatever is offered, even if it be coarse or poor food, entering in accordance with worldly customs and manifesting in this way.”

"The merit of the Buddha's virtues is inexhaustible, and none can surpass it; yet when the Buddha enters the city for alms and returns with an empty bowl, he does so by conforming to worldly customs, manifesting such a display."

"The merits and blessings of the Buddha are inexhaustible; were he to desire fine garments renowned throughout heaven and earth, he could obtain them all. Yet he wears robes of patched rags, conforming to the worldly customs of the age and manifesting himself in such a manner."

"The Buddha could obtain houses, couches, bedding, and the rare treasures of the heavens above and the earth below, as well as palatial dwellings; yet he appears among the people of the world, dwelling in the open air and meditating upon mats of grass, conforming to worldly customs and manifesting himself in such a manner."

"The Buddha, by means of his majestic spiritual power, can blow upon the waters of the ocean until they are completely dried up; yet when he sees rain falling, he holds up a parasol. He manifests such things in order to conform to the worldly customs."

"In a single moment of thought, the Buddha can cause many thousands of millions of billions of māras to be unaware of his location; he manifests as a person being harassed by māras, entering according to worldly customs and conventions, and displays himself in such a manner."

“The Buddha fully understands all the sūtras and dharmas of the innumerable Buddhas of the ten directions; he manifests himself by responding to repeated questions and enters into accordance with worldly customs, manifesting himself in such a manner.”

“Because the Buddha, out of compassion for the ten directions, appears in the world with the desire to teach and deliver beings, and further manifests so that people may make offerings and obtain immeasurable merit; he enters according to worldly customs and manifests such things.”

“The Buddha has no fundamental basis; he manifests his body in accordance with the colors favored by the world. Though his essence is fundamentally one, he enters into worldly customs and manifests himself accordingly.”

“Even if the sounds of thunder and lightning from the ten directions were gathered together to form a single sound, it could not move a single hair of the Buddha. Manifesting entry into the *dhyāna-samādhi*, he enters according to worldly customs and conventions; it is thus that he manifests.”

"The various dharmas of the sutras are fundamentally nameless; yet the Buddha reveals to people the countless dharmas of the sutras, entering according to worldly customs and manifesting them in such a way."

"Having fundamentally severed all conceptualizations regarding the Buddha and remaining constantly inseparable from samādhi, he manifests to teach various kinds of sūtras and dharmas to people, entering according to worldly customs and manifesting in such ways."

"Regarding what the Buddha performed in previous lives, the good and evil deeds cannot be reaped in that same body; they must inevitably be reaped in a subsequent life. The Buddha shows people that what one does oneself, one receives oneself; he manifests in this manner by conforming to worldly customs and conventions."

“The Buddha knows that the world is fundamentally non-existent and that all things possessed by people are fundamentally formless; yet the Buddha manifests the deliverance of countless beings, entering according to the worldly customs and manifesting himself in such a way.”

“The Buddha knows that all sūtras and dharmas are fundamentally empty and fundamentally non-existent; yet, manifesting as people undergo further birth and death, he enters according to worldly customs and manifests in such a manner.”

"In reality, there are no matters of this world or future worlds; it is only because the Buddha perceives that people believe in this world and future worlds that he conforms to worldly customs and manifests such things."

"The five aggregates, the six sense-bases, and the four great elements are combined into one; fundamentally they do not exist. Yet the Buddha manifests as humans, in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, entering according to worldly customs and manifesting in such ways."

"Fundamentally, there are no people of the past, future, or present; it is the Buddha who manifests among those in the five paths of birth and death, entering according to worldly customs and manifesting in such a manner."
“The Buddha has fully demonstrated that all delusion is exhausted; he manifests the fundamental nature of giving to people and enters into worldly customs to manifest such things.

Regarding the sutras and dharmas of the past, future, and present, the Buddha knows their origin; the Buddha demonstrates to people what can be spoken and what cannot be spoken, entering into worldly customs to manifest such things.”

“The Buddha knows that the beginning and end of all sūtras are entirely profound; yet the Buddha distinguishes them and speaks of their respective matters, entering according to the worldly customs and manifesting himself in such ways.”

"What the Buddha speaks is without any discrepancy; he teaches the Dharma of the Four Truths according to how people understand it, entering into worldly conventions and manifesting them in such a manner."

“The community of bhikṣus is difficult to cause dissension; even if tens of billions of Māras and various evils were to come, they could not destroy the community of bhikṣus. When the Buddha appears to cause dissension within the community of bhikṣus, he does so by conforming to worldly customs and manifesting such a display.”

“The Dharma of the sutras is fundamentally without origin; there is no one from whom it is learned, nor is there anyone who does not learn it. The Buddha manifests the Dharma of the sutras for people—this as receiving precepts and this as not receiving precepts—entering according to worldly customs and manifesting in such ways.”

“Even emptiness is empty; there is neither bondage nor liberation from the world. The Buddha shows people the way to transcendence, yet he enters according to worldly customs and manifests himself in such a manner.”

“The Buddha’s parinirvāṇa has no destination; the Arhat’s parinirvāṇa has no destination. When the Buddha teaches the Dharma to people, he enters according to the customs of the world and manifests himself in such a manner.”

“The Buddha taught that there is neither arising nor ceasing; this is the essential point. There is nothing to be gained and nothing to be lost; he enters into accordance with worldly customs and manifests himself in such a way.”
“The Buddha taught that *nirvāṇa* is like the extinguishing of a lamp: it has no form, there being only the name.
The sutras and the Dharma cannot be destroyed; they enter into accordance with worldly customs and manifest themselves in such a way.”

“The Buddha fully knows that all sūtras and dharmas are fundamentally formless; yet the Buddha manifests to people by preaching a vast multitude of sūtras and dharmas, entering according to the worldly customs and manifesting in such a manner.”

"The minds of all Buddhas are entirely free from obstruction; they never depart from samādhi, yet they manifest the arising of thoughts in humans, entering into worldly customs and conventions to display such phenomena."

“The Buddha has exhausted all evils and possesses every perfection; yet the Buddha manifests to people as if his evils were not yet exhausted, entering according to worldly customs and manifesting in such a manner.”

“The Buddha’s bodily actions, verbal expressions, and mental thoughts should always be accompanied by wisdom; this is the foundation. When the Buddha manifests before people and causes bhikṣus to preach the sūtras, or when he himself wishes to hear them, he enters according to worldly customs and manifests in such ways.”

"The wisdom realized by the Buddha has no bottomless abyss; the past, future, and present are fundamentally empty. Yet the Buddha manifests and speaks the Dharma for people, teaching each according to their inclinations and entering into worldly customs to manifest in such ways."

"All Buddhas are of one body, taking the sutras and Dharma as their body; the Buddha manifests as a human being to preach the sutras and Dharma, entering according to the customs of the world and manifesting in such a manner."

"Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, and those on the path who have not yet attained [the goal] manifest death and birth and attain nirvāṇa; they enter according to worldly customs and manifest in such a manner."

“The Buddha manifests for the arhats and preaches the Dharma in its entirety; although he knows it to be complete, it does not equal *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). He enters according to worldly customs and manifests himself in such a manner.”

"The Buddha’s wisdom is unsurpassed; he fully knows that there is nothing past, future, or present. When the Buddha manifests by means of causes and conditions to preach the Dharma, he enters according to the worldly customs and manifests in such a manner."

“If there are those who wish to know the Buddha and understand the Buddha-dharma, they must enter the fundamental boundaries of the sutras; such a person is one who has realized the Buddha, entering in accordance with worldly customs and manifesting in this way.”
“The Bodhisattva likewise does not enter the mother’s womb, nor does he emerge from the mother’s womb.
Why is this? Because the fundamental realm of the sūtra-dharma has nothing into which it does not penetrate.”
The Bodhisattva manifests entering his mother’s womb; he follows worldly customs and enters therein, manifesting in this way.

"There is the joy of the dharma of non-arising, and all dharmas of the sūtras likewise have no place of arising"; when the Bodhisattva manifests being born for the first time, he follows worldly customs and enters therein, manifesting in this way.

"The womb of the Bodhisattva’s mother is in the concentration of emptiness, containing the realm of a single Buddha; yet each Bodhisattva manifests birth through human causes and conditions, entering according to worldly customs and conventions, and thus makes such a demonstration."

“The Buddha’s manifested bodies are infinite and beyond calculation, reaching everywhere throughout all buddha-fields; yet the Buddha-body neither increases nor decreases, entering according to the worldly customs and manifesting in such a manner.”

“The Bodhisattva constantly manifests birth without interruption; though eternally abiding in the primordial non-arising, he does not undergo toil or hardship, yet he enters according to worldly customs and manifests in such a manner.”

“The wisdom, merit, and majestic spiritual power of the Buddha are beyond calculation; yet the Buddha manifests limits such as long or short stature to enable people to know him, entering according to worldly customs and manifesting himself in such ways.”
“The fundamental realm of the sūtra-dharma cannot be surpassed, for the past, future, and present are all empty.
The Buddha manifests as a Honored One among men and presents the sūtra-dharma by conforming to worldly customs; he displays it in this manner.”

"Fundamentally there is neither arising nor ceasing; they fully enter the original realm. When the Buddha manifests within the sphere of human experience during its decline, he enters according to worldly customs and manifests in such a manner."

“The Dharma of the sutras fundamentally has no place from which it arises; it abides without form. Yet the Buddha manifests the Dharma of the sutras, entering according to the customs and habits of the world, and thus makes such a display.”

“Contemplating original non-existence, there is neither that which is seen nor that which is viewed; yet the Buddha views all people, seeing them all, understanding them all, and knowing them all, entering according to the worldly customs and manifesting in such a manner.”

"The various sūtras and dharmas have no creator and are not produced; the Buddha manifests to people that the sūtras and dharmas are fundamentally unproduced, yet he enters according to worldly customs and manifests them in such a way."

"Nirvāṇa and emptiness have neither form nor sound, nor do they possess names; yet the Buddha manifests the four great elements, forms, and sounds, entering according to the worldly conventions and manifesting in this manner."

"The power of the Buddha is peerless and beyond calculation; it never diminishes nor comes to an end. Yet, appearing as an aged man seeking those to serve him, he enters into accordance with worldly customs and manifests himself in such a manner."

“The Buddha’s compassion is all-pervasive and equal; it shall never come to an end or reach a point of exhaustion. When the Buddha appears to act as if he were a fool, it is not that he should engage in such affairs; rather, he enters according to worldly customs and manifests himself in this way.”

“The Buddha has fully accomplished and perfected all merits; yet when the Buddha manifests only a small portion of his merits, he does so by entering into accordance with worldly customs, manifesting himself in such a way.”

"The fundamental source is without arising; from within it, nothing further is produced. That the Buddha manifests three gates is because he enters according to worldly customs and appears in such a manner."

“The Buddha’s manifestations are fundamentally unimpeded; his merit and blessings are such that none can surpass them. When the Buddha appears before people who offer gifts, he does not accept them but merely acts as if satisfied, demonstrating non-attachment. He enters into accordance with worldly customs and manifests himself in this manner.”

"If there are people who recite the Buddha's name with utmost sincerity and a wholesome mind, the Buddha will immediately manifest before them. Yet the Buddha has no fixed location; when he manifests his body to practice the bodhisattva path, he enters according to the worldly customs and manifests himself in such ways."
“The Buddha delivers and liberates incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* beings, yet he does not deliver even a single person.
Why is this? Because they are fundamentally non-existent; it is only by conforming to worldly customs that he manifests such a display.”

"Regarding the *Buddharatnagarbha Sūtra*, anyone who hears it will find no lack of peace and security; they shall transcend countless billions of kalpas. Such is the conduct practiced by these bodhisattvas life after life for the sake of the people of the ten directions."

Throughout successive lifetimes, the Bodhisattva practices the sutras and precepts, never committing a transgression; by means of this, he attains the wisdom of a Buddha, and one who accords with such practice will swiftly attain Buddhahood.
The Bodhisattva practices loving-kindness and compassion, benefiting the ten directions infinitely; those who perform such deeds will swiftly attain Buddhahood.
Who would hear this and not practice it?
The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is so sublime that whoever hears this sutra and its Dharma will all attain transcendence.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and the other bodhisattvas were all filled with joy; they came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Hundred Treasures Stored Within.
